TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) -- A well-known Iranian filmmaker has written an open letter calling for the release of journalist Roxana Saberi. In a letter, Iranian filmmaker Bahman Ghobadi blames himself for urging Roxana Saberi to stay in Iran. Bahman Ghobadi said he kept quiet about the arrest and conviction of the Iranian-American journalist at the request of her family. After Saberi was convicted last weekend and sentenced to an eight-year prison sentence, he said he felt he had to do something. He told CNN that Saberi, whom he described as his fiancee, is caught in a "game of politics." In his letter, which has been posted by the International Campaign for Human Rights in Iran, Ghobadi blames himself for urging Saberi to stay in Iran despite her desire to leave. Also, he writes, "My letter is a desperate call to all statesmen ... and to all those who can do something to help." "From the other side of the ocean, the Americans have protested against her imprisonment, because she is an American citizen," he writes. "But I say no, she is Iranian, and she loves Iran. I beg you, let her go! I beg you not to throw her in the midst of your political games! She is too weak and too pure to take part in your games. Let me be present at her trial, sit next to her wise father and gentle mother, and testify she is without guilt or reproach." The 40-year-old filmmaker said that Saberi was planning to leave the country, but he kept her from leaving until his latest film -- which will be shown at this year's Cannes film festival -- was completed. Ghobadi won the 2000 Golden Camera award at the Cannes festival for his feature film, "A Time for Drunken Horses." Saberi, 31, was sentenced Saturday to eight years in prison after a one-day trial that was closed to the public. The decision prompted sharp denunciations from President Barack Obama, as well as other U.S. and international officials. Iranian officials initially said Saberi was held for buying a bottle of wine. The Foreign Ministry later said she was detained for reporting without proper accreditation. On April 9, word emerged that Saberi had been charged with espionage. Saberi's lawyer has said he will appeal the verdict. Judiciary Chief Ayatollah Hashemi Shahroudi has ordered the head of Tehran's Justice Department to make sure the appeals process is quick and fair. Ghobadi wrote that he is "optimistic about her release, and I firmly hope the verdict will be canceled in the next stage of the trial." "My Iranian girl with Japanese eyes and an American ID, is in jail. Shame on me! Shame on us!" CNN's Igor Krotov and Shirzad Bozorghmehr contributed to this report.

"She is far too fragile to endure the harsh conditions of prison," Ghobadi wrote, adding that he feels personally responsible for encouraging her to stay in the country to complete her research. "I cannot live with the thought of her suffering in a cell for crimes she did not commit."

Ghobadi, an internationally recognized filmmaker best known for award-winning movies such as *Turtles Can Fly* and *A Time for Drunken Horses*, revealed that he and Saberi had planned to move to Europe together once she finished her book on Iranian society. 

The filmmaker's public intervention adds a deeply personal element to an issue that has escalated into a major diplomatic flashpoint between Washington and Tehran. 

U.S. President Barack Obama has expressed "deep concern" over Saberi's detention, stating he is confident she was not involved in espionage. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton has also repeatedly called on Iranian authorities to dismiss the charges and allow Saberi to return to the United States.

Iranian judicial officials have insisted that Saberi will receive a fair trial, though proceedings in Iran’s Revolutionary Courts are typically held behind closed doors.

For Ghobadi, the appeal is a desperate attempt to save the woman he loves before it is too late.

"I am begging the authorities, the judiciary, and anyone who has power in Iran to look at Roxana not as a political pawn, but as an innocent human being," Ghobadi wrote. "Please, let her go free."

**TEHRAN** — Renowned Iranian filmmaker Bahman Ghobadi has issued an emotional public plea for the release of his fiancée, Iranian-American journalist Roxana Saberi, following her conviction by an Iranian court on charges of spying for the United States. Saberi was handed an eight-year prison sentence following a swift, closed-door trial, triggering international condemnation and deepening diplomatic tensions between Washington and Tehran.

Saberi, a 31-year-old dual citizen who has reported for National Public Radio (NPR), the BBC, and Fox News, was sentenced by a Revolutionary Court in mid-April 2009. The severity of the sentence—the harshest handed to a dual national on security charges in recent years—sent shockwaves through the international journalistic community and prompted an extraordinary public intervention by Ghobadi, one of Iran's most celebrated directors.

---

### **Bahman Ghobadi’s Public Letter: "She Is Innocent"**

In an open letter addressed to Iranian officials and distributed to international media outlets, Ghobadi revealed for the first time his deep personal connection to Saberi, describing her as his fiancée and creative partner. Ghobadi, best known for his award-winning films *A Time for Drunken Horses* and *No One Knows About Persian Cats*, broke his silence to defend Saberi’s character and work, vehemently denying that she engaged in espionage.

"Roxana is innocent," Ghobadi wrote in the impassioned letter. "She is too gentle, too pure, and too naive to be involved in these dangerous political games. Her only crime was her love for Iran and her desire to write a honest book about its people."

Ghobadi detailed how Saberi had spent the last six years living in Tehran, working on a book about Iranian society and culture, while also collaborating with him on film projects. He described her as a dedicated researcher who operated entirely in the open.

"She came to Iran with a heart full of enthusiasm to understand her father’s homeland," Ghobadi wrote. "She is like a bird trapped in a cage. I call upon the authorities, upon anyone with power and a conscience, to release her. Do not let her youth be destroyed in Evin Prison."

Ghobadi also expressed profound guilt over her detention, revealing that Saberi had considered leaving Iran prior to her arrest but stayed partly due to his encouragement to finish her research and film collaborations.

---

### **Background on Charges and Secret Trial**

Saberi was initially detained in late January 2009. Iranian authorities initially gave conflicting reasons for her arrest, suggesting at first that she had been detained for purchasing alcohol—a crime under Iran’s Islamic law—and later claiming she was practicing journalism without valid press credentials, which had been revoked by the government in 2006.

However, in early April, the charges were dramatically escalated when Iranian prosecutors officially accused her of espionage. Iranian judicial spokesman Alireza Jamshidi alleged that Saberi had used her press access to collect classified documents and pass them to American intelligence agencies. 

Her trial, which took place in early April, was conducted entirely behind closed doors at Tehran's Revolutionary Court. According to her lawyer, Abdolsamad Khorramshahi, the legal proceeding lasted less than an hour. Saberi was denied standard legal protections, and her defense team was given minimal time to review the evidence against her. 

Following the secret trial, the court sentenced her to eight years in Evin Prison, Tehran's notorious facility known for holding political prisoners and foreign detainees.

---

### **International Backlash and Political Context**

The conviction sparked swift outrage from foreign leaders and human rights organizations. U.S. President Barack Obama expressed "deep disappointment" over the ruling, stating he was confident Saberi was not involved in espionage activities. U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton called the charges "baseless" and demanded her immediate release.

"We are deeply concerned about her well-being and safety," Clinton stated, emphasizing that Washington would continue to push through diplomatic channels, utilizing Swiss intermediaries who represent U.S. interests in Tehran.

Saberi, a former Miss North Dakota and graduate of Northwestern University and the University of Cambridge, moved to Iran in 2003. Her father, Reza Saberi, an Iranian immigrant to the United States, traveled to Tehran alongside her mother, Akiko, to plead for her release. He reported that his daughter had been tricked into making a confession under duress, which she later recanted in court.

Political analysts note that Saberi’s arrest and harsh sentencing come at a delicate political juncture. The Obama administration had recently signaled a desire for diplomatic engagement with Iran, but hardline factions within Iran’s judiciary and security apparatus appear eager to derail potential normalization efforts ahead of Iran's upcoming presidential election.

Ghobadi’s public stance is considered uniquely dangerous for a high-profile figure living inside Iran, where criticizing the judiciary can carry severe personal and professional consequences. Nevertheless, the director maintained that silence was no longer an option.

"I cannot sit back and watch her life be ruined," Ghobadi’s letter concluded. "Roxana belongs to the world of art and truth, not to a prison cell."

Saberi’s legal team has formally filed an appeal against the eight-year sentence, with Iranian judicial officials indicating that a review of the case will take place in the coming weeks.

***

*Reporting compiled from dispatch services including The Associated Press, Reuters, Agence France-Presse (AFP), and CNN.*

Ghobadi’s letter, combined with intense diplomatic pressure from the U.S. and European nations, put significant international pressure on the Iranian judiciary.

counterfactuals.prompt: Act as a foreign correspondent and provide a news piece about the political and human rights fallout of Roxana Saberi's trial in Iran, highlighting Bahman Ghobadi's emotional appeal.
counterfactuals.output:
**TEHRAN** — The swift and secretive conviction of Iranian-American journalist Roxana Saberi has sent a deep chill through Iran’s intellectual community and sparked a diplomatic firestorm, casting a long shadow over Washington’s recent attempts to open dialogue with Tehran. 

Saberi, a 31-year-old former Miss North Dakota who has worked for NPR and the BBC, was sentenced to eight years in prison by a Revolutionary Court on charges of espionage. Human rights organizations have roundly condemned the trial, which lasted just one day behind closed doors, as a sham—a stark reminder of the Iranian judiciary’s routine disregard for due process.

Beyond the geopolitical posturing between the Obama administration and Iranian hardliners, the trial has taken a devastating personal turn, underscored by an extraordinary and passionate appeal from one of Iran’s most celebrated filmmakers, Bahman Ghobadi.

In an open letter released to international media, Ghobadi—director of the acclaimed films *A Time for Drunken Horses* and *No One Knows About Persian Cats*—revealed for the first time that he and Saberi were engaged to be married. Breaking the silence often maintained by those fearful of judicial reprisal, Ghobadi issued a raw, emotional plea for her release, describing a woman captivated not by state secrets, but by the rich, complex culture of her father’s homeland.

"Roxana is innocent," Ghobadi wrote, his words echoing across international artistic circles. "She loved Iran so much that she spent years here, quietly working on a book about the Iranian people. She came to understand this country, to love it, and now she is being punished for that love."

Ghobadi detailed Saberi’s fragile physical and mental state inside Tehran’s notorious Evin Prison, appealing directly to the Iranian authorities' sense of mercy, while expressing his own profound helplessness. His public intervention is a rare and dangerous move in a country where criticizing the Revolutionary Courts can easily land a citizen in an adjacent prison cell. 

The fallout from Saberi’s conviction extends far beyond the emotional turmoil of her family and fiancé. Human rights advocates view the harsh sentence as a direct message from Iranian intelligence apparatuses to the country's vibrant, albeit heavily restricted, press corps.

"Saberi’s case demonstrates the absolute vulnerability of dual-nationals and foreign correspondents in Iran," said a Dubai-based researcher for Human Rights Watch. "The message from the hardline establishment is clear: foreign journalists operate here purely at the whim of the state, and their freedom can be revoked the moment political leverage is needed."

Politically, the timing could not be worse for those hoping for a thaw in US-Iran relations. US President Barack Obama, who recently extended a diplomatic olive branch to Tehran in a televised New Year’s address, expressed "deep disappointment" over the verdict, insisting that Saberi was engaging in standard journalistic activities, not espionage. 

Analysts here in the region suggest that Saberi has become a pawn in a larger internal power struggle. With Iran’s presidential elections approaching in June, hardline factions within the regime appear eager to sabotage any potential rapprochement with the West, using Saberi to assert their control over foreign policy and security matters.

As international pressure mounts—with European governments, media freedom groups, and cultural figures joining Ghobadi’s chorus—Saberi’s lawyers have lodged an official appeal. 

For now, however, the young journalist remains behind the high walls of Evin Prison. And in the cafes and film studios of Tehran, a heavy silence has settled, broken only by the courageous voice of a fiancé refusing to let the world forget the human cost of a regime’s political games.

*This is [Your Name], reporting for Foreign News.*
